prompt.context: Your client is the owner of a Patty Joint (PJ) franchise in the small town of Shelton, Connecticut (population 40K). The restaurant's revenues are trending downward but costs are stable.
prompt.question: What are your thoughts on: 1) The cause of the issue, and 2) How to achieve growth of the business?

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any changes in customer tastes, menu, food quality, or suppliers?
clarifying_info.a: No changes in any of those areas.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any new competition nearby?
clarifying_info.a: A new competitor, FinerFoods Restaurant, opened across the street. It is a fast food 'plus' style restaurant serving not only burgers but also a broader menu (chicken, pasta, burritos) with tablecloths and waiter service, and has a family-friendly atmosphere.

clarifying_info.q: Who are Patty Joint's main customer segments?
clarifying_info.a: There are two main customer segments: 1) Business customers for lunch (60% of clientele) and 2) Families for dinner (40% of clientele). Patty Joint is losing both segments to the new competition.

framework: Diagnose the root cause of declining revenues — rule out internal factors (menu, quality, pricing, staffing) before looking externally
Identify the competitive threat — FinerFoods opening across the street with broader menu, waiter service, and family atmosphere
Segment the customer base — business lunch vs. family dinner — and quantify profitability of each segment
Gather customer feedback to understand why each segment is defecting and what they value
Prioritize the more profitable segment and design targeted retention/growth solutions within corporate policy constraints
Summarize cause, prioritized segment, and recommended actions

questions.prompt: Which customer segment is more important and more profitable — business lunch or family dinner?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use weighted average math to back-solve for the dinner segment profit. Lunch is 60% of customers at $8 profit; overall average is $10. Solving for dinner profit identifies the more profitable segment. Dinner customers are more profitable ($13 vs $8), making them the higher-priority segment to retain.

math.answer: Dinner segment profit = $13/customer, which is more profitable than lunch at $8/customer.

questions.prompt: If the total average profit margin is 50%, what is the overall average revenue per customer?
questions.guidance: Candidate divides overall average profit by profit margin to get revenue per customer.

questions.prompt: FinerFoods' revenues are 20% higher and costs are 10% higher than PJ's overall average customer. What is FinerFoods' average profit per customer?
questions.guidance: Candidate should index PJ's revenue ($20) and cost ($10) by the given percentages to compute FinerFoods' profit, then compare to PJ's $10 average.

math.setup: PJ revenue = $20, PJ cost = $20 - $10 = $10 (derived from 50% margin). FinerFoods: Revenue = 1.20 × $20; Costs = 1.10 × $10
math.answer: FinerFoods earns $13 profit per customer vs. PJ's $10 — FinerFoods has a more profitable business per customer.

questions.prompt: How would Patty Joint determine why their customers are leaving?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify multiple research methods and note potential biases.

questions.prompt: You now have a chance to create customer survey questions. State whom the survey is tailored toward and your most important question.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the two defecting segments (business lunch, family dinner) and craft targeted questions around the key decision factors for each. Strong candidates note the need to avoid bias (e.g., equal mix of regular vs. one-time customers).

questions.prompt: Based on the survey results and given that you cannot hire additional service staff or change menu offerings, which segment would you focus on and what solutions would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Focus on the more profitable family dinner segment ($13/customer profit). Solutions should address what families value — price perception, reduced cleanup hassle, children's engagement — without adding staff or changing the menu. Business lunch segment perceives FinerFoods as faster even though actual time is similar, making it harder to win back without service changes.

brainstorming.prompt: How would Patty Joint determine why their customers are leaving?

categories.name: Primary Research
ideas: Customer satisfaction survey — equal mix of regular and one-time customers to reduce bias
Exit interviews with customers leaving or switching to FinerFoods
Focus groups with defecting family and business lunch customers

categories.name: Internal / Corporate Data
ideas: Ask corporate HQ for performance data from other PJ franchises that faced a nearby FinerFoods or similar competitor opening
Compare same-store sales trends at comparable PJ locations without new competition

categories.name: Secondary Research
ideas: Industry publications on fast-food competitive dynamics
Market research on consumer preferences in fast-casual dining
Social media and review sites (Yelp, Google) for qualitative feedback

recommendation: The primary cause of Patty Joint's revenue decline is the opening of FinerFoods across the street, which is drawing away both business lunch and family dinner customers
Focus retention efforts on the family dinner segment, which is more profitable at $13/customer vs. $8 for business lunch

Invest in making PJ more attractive to families within corporate policy: add children's entertainment (playground, clown), promote birthday and special event packages, reduce packaging to minimize cleanup burden for parents
risks: Business lunch segment may continue to defect if speed/convenience perception gap vs. FinerFoods persists
Family-focused investments require capital expenditure with uncertain payback period
Corporate policy constraints (no new staff, no menu changes) limit the breadth of solutions available
next_steps: Conduct formal customer survey segmented by lunch vs. dinner customers to validate survey findings at scale
Benchmark other PJ franchises that have faced similar competitive threats for proven response playbooks
Model ROI on family entertainment investments (e.g., playground cost vs. incremental dinner covers and revenue)
